Study guide · Autumn 2018 · Andrew Ng

The Landscape of Machine Learning

Lecture 1 is the only lecture in CS229 that does not teach an algorithm. Instead it draws the map: what a learning problem is, the three ways a learning problem can be posed, and the two cross-cutting concerns — theory and strategy — that decide whether any of it works in practice. This guide keeps only the academic content, reconstructs each idea at the level of precision the later lectures will assume, and marks the places where Ng states something without justifying it yet.

00 · Orientation

The 60-second map

One taxonomy, five boxes. Everything else in the course hangs off it. Read this first; come back to it whenever a later lecture feels like it arrived from nowhere.

Ng organises the whole syllabus around a single question: what is the learner given, and what is it asked to produce? Answer that three different ways and you get the three learning paradigms. Two further blocks — learning theory and deep learning — are not paradigms at all; they cut across the other three. Mis-filing deep learning as a fourth paradigm is the most common error students make with this material.

The one sentence to memorise

The paradigm is fixed by the supervision signal, not by the algorithm and not by the model. Labels present → supervised. No labels → unsupervised. A scalar reward arriving after a sequence of your own decisions → reinforcement.

0.1 · Vocabulary

Notation you need before minute one

Ng writes most of this on the board in Lecture 2 and then never re-defines it. It is used informally throughout Lecture 1, so it is worth pinning down now.

Trap · the superscript

x(2)x^{(2)}x(2) is the second training example. x2x^{2}x2 is xxx squared. x2x_{2}x2​ is the second feature. Three different objects, one character apart. Every CS229 problem set exploits this at least once.

Gap · the assumption nobody states in Lecture 1

Every claim of the form “the algorithm learned something useful” silently assumes that training data and future data are drawn from the same distribution, and drawn independently — the i.i.d. assumption. Write it down now: (x(i),y(i)) ∼iid D,i=1,…,m(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\ \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\ \mathcal{D},\qquad i=1,\dots,m(x(i),y(i)) ∼iid D,i=1,…,m and the test point (x,y)∼D(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}(x,y)∼D too. Nothing in the course generalises without it, and Lecture 9 (learning theory) is essentially the study of what this assumption buys you. If the distribution shifts — you trained on daytime photos and deploy at night — every guarantee in CS229 is void.

0.2 · Definitions

What “learning” means

Two classical definitions, forty years apart. Ng quotes the informal one; the formal one is the one you can actually compute with.

Arthur Samuel (1959), informal. Machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. Samuel wrote a checkers player that played tens of thousands of games against itself and became better at checkers than Samuel was — the historical point being that the programmer need not be the expert.

Tom Mitchell (1997), operational. A computer program is said to learn from experience EEE with respect to some task TTT and performance measure PPP, if its performance on TTT, as measured by PPP, improves with experience EEE. This version is useful because it forces you to name three things before you write any code:

Housing pricesTumour diagnosisCheckers
TTT — taskpredict price from arealabel a tumour benign/malignantplay a game of checkers
EEE — experiencemmm past salesmmm diagnosed patientsgames played against itself
PPP — performancemean squared errormisclassification ratefraction of games won
Gap · why the definition matters more than it looks

Mitchell’s PPP is where most real projects go wrong, and Lecture 1 does not dwell on it. Choosing PPP = accuracy on a dataset where 99 % of tumours are benign makes “always predict benign” a 99 %-accurate model and a useless one. The performance measure is a modelling decision with the same status as the choice of hypothesis class — you will meet this again as the difference between the loss you optimise and the metric you care about.

01 · Paradigm one

Supervised learning

The bulk of the course. You are handed the right answers for mmm examples and asked to produce a function that gives right answers for examples you have never seen.

Formally: you are given a training set {(x(i),y(i))}i=1m\big\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\big\}_{i=1}^{m}{(x(i),y(i))}i=1m​ with x(i)∈Xx^{(i)}\in\mathcal{X}x(i)∈X and y(i)∈Yy^{(i)}\in\mathcal{Y}y(i)∈Y, and you must output a hypothesis h:X→Yh:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}h:X→Y that predicts well on new draws from the same distribution. The word supervised refers to the presence of yyy — a supervisor who has already labelled the answers.

Regression: the target is continuous

Ng’s opening example is house prices: each example is a house, the input xxx is its living area, and the target yyy is the price it sold for. Because yyy is a real number, Y=R\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}Y=R and the problem is a regression problem. The task is to produce a curve through the cloud of points and then read predictions off it.

Notice what the picture already commits you to. Choosing “a straight line” means the hypothesis is hθ(x)=θ0+θ1xh_{\theta}(x)=\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}xhθ​(x)=θ0​+θ1​x, so learning has been reduced to choosing two numbers. Choosing “a quadratic” means three numbers. The learning algorithm never invents the form of hhh; it only picks the parameters inside a form you supplied.

Try it · what fitting actually means

Below, the two sliders are θ0\theta_{0}θ0​ and θ1\theta_{1}θ1​ — the entire content of “the model”. Every vertical grey stub is a residual hθ(x(i))−y(i)h_{\theta}(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}hθ​(x(i))−y(i), and the number in the corner is the mean squared error. Try to beat the least-squares solution by hand before pressing Fit.

Classification: the target is discrete

The second example is breast-tumour diagnosis: given features of a tumour, predict whether it is malignant (y=1y=1y=1) or benign (y=0y=0y=0). Now Y={0,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\}Y={0,1}, a finite set, and the problem is classification. The picture changes accordingly: instead of a curve through the points you are drawing a decision boundary that cuts the input space into regions.

Ng pushes the idea one step further. If two features help, why not three, or a hundred, or infinitely many? An algorithm that can work with an infinite-dimensional feature vector sounds impossible, and the promise that the support vector machine does exactly that (via the kernel trick, Lecture 7) is the hook he leaves dangling at the end of the classification segment.

Try it · one feature versus two

The same 60 patients, twice. In 1 feature mode you may only choose a threshold on tumour size; the error count bottoms out well above zero. Switch to 2 features and rotate the boundary: the same points become separable. The error counter is the whole argument.

Misclassified: —

Other supervised problems Ng names

  • Autonomous steering. Input: a camera image of the road. Output: a steering angle. A human drives for a few minutes while the system records (image, steering angle) pairs; the learned hhh then steers. Y=R\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}Y=R, so despite the exotic input this is plain regression.
  • Spam filtering. Input: an email. Output: spam or not. Binary classification, and the running example for Naive Bayes in Lecture 5.
  • Handwritten digits. Ten classes rather than two — multiclass classification, which Lecture 4 handles with softmax regression.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 1 · regression versus classification is about Y\mathcal{Y}Y, not about the algorithm

Students leave Lecture 1 believing “lines are regression, boundaries are classification”. Both pictures show a straight line. The distinction is entirely in the codomain: in Fig. 3 the line is the prediction h(x)h(x)h(x); in Fig. 5 the line is the level set {x:h(x)=0.5}\{x: h(x)=0.5\}{x:h(x)=0.5} of a prediction you cannot see in the plot. Same geometry, different meaning. And note the name: logistic regression (Lecture 3) is a classification algorithm.

Gap 2 · where the labels come from

The lecture treats yyy as simply given. In practice, obtaining yyy is the expensive part of a supervised project: someone must biopsy the tumour, drive the car, or read the email. Three consequences worth knowing before you choose a project: (a) label noise is normal — two radiologists disagree, so even a perfect hhh has non-zero error; (b) labels can be systematically biased by who produced them; (c) the amount of labelled data available, not the algorithm, is usually what caps performance. This is why the semi-supervised and self-supervised settings exist, and why unsupervised methods stay interesting.

Trap · “more features is always better”

Fig. 5 shows a second feature rescuing a hopeless problem, which invites the conclusion that features are free. They are not. Each added feature adds a parameter to fit, and with nnn comparable to mmm a linear model can fit any labelling of the training set — including the noise. That is the overfitting story of §04, and the reason regularisation exists.

02 · Paradigm two

Unsupervised learning

Same xxx’s, no yyy’s. The instruction is not “predict this” but “find something interesting in here”, and making that instruction precise is the whole difficulty.

The training set is now {x(i)}i=1m\{x^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{m}{x(i)}i=1m​ — inputs only. Because there is no target to be right or wrong about, there is no error rate to minimise, and the algorithm must be told what “structure” means by the shape of its objective. Different definitions of structure give different algorithms.

Clustering, and the examples Ng uses

  • News aggregation. Thousands of articles arrive each hour; grouping the ones covering the same story requires no labels, only a notion of similarity between documents.
  • Gene expression. Rows are individuals, columns are genes, entries are expression levels. Clustering the rows discovers subpopulations nobody defined in advance — the point being that the categories are an output, not an input.
  • Market segmentation. Grouping customers to find segments a marketing team never wrote down.
  • Social networks. Given who talks to whom, find the tightly connected communities.

The algorithm behind the picture is kkk-means, which Lecture 14 derives properly. Its logic is two alternating steps, and seeing them alternate is worth more than the pseudocode:

The kkk-means loop
  1. Pick kkk and initialise kkk cluster centroids μ1,…,μk\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{k}μ1​,…,μk​ at random points. kkk is your choice. Nothing in the data supplies it.
  2. Assign. Give every example to its nearest centroid: c(i):=arg⁡min⁡j ∥x(i)−μj∥2c^{(i)} := \arg\min_{j}\ \big\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{j}\big\rVert^{2}c(i):=argjmin​ ​x(i)−μj​​2 Each point looks around and joins the closest group. Centroids are held fixed.
  3. Update. Move each centroid to the mean of the points now assigned to it: μj:=∑i=1m1{c(i)=j} x(i)∑i=1m1{c(i)=j}\mu_{j} := \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{1}\{c^{(i)}=j\}\,x^{(i)}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{1}\{c^{(i)}=j\}}μj​:=∑i=1m​1{c(i)=j}∑i=1m​1{c(i)=j}x(i)​ Assignments are held fixed. The mean is the point minimising summed squared distance to the group — which is why squared distance and the arithmetic mean appear together.
  4. Repeat 2–3 until no assignment changes. Each step can only decrease the distortion ∑i∥x(i)−μc(i)∥2\sum_i\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{c^{(i)}}\rVert^{2}∑i​∥x(i)−μc(i)​∥2, and there are finitely many assignments, so the loop terminates. It terminates at a local minimum, which is why you restart it several times.
Try it · watch Lloyd’s algorithm converge

Press Assign and Update alternately and watch the distortion fall, or press Run. Two things to notice: the distortion never increases, and a bad random seed can leave two centroids sharing one blob while a real cluster goes unclaimed. Re-seed a few times with k=3k=3k=3 and you will see it happen.

Distortion: —

The cocktail-party problem

Two people speak at once in a room; two microphones stand in different corners. Each microphone records a different mixture of the two voices. Given only the two mixtures, recover the two voices. In matrix form, with sources s∈R2s\in\mathbb{R}^{2}s∈R2 and an unknown mixing matrix AAA,

x=A s,observe x, recover s=A−1x=Wx.x = A\,s,\qquad \text{observe } x,\ \text{recover } s = A^{-1}x = Wx.x=As,observe x, recover s=A−1x=Wx.

The algorithm — independent component analysis — must estimate WWW without ever seeing sss. It is unsupervised in the purest sense: there is no label anywhere, and the only thing the method assumes is that the sources are statistically independent and non-Gaussian.

Trap · the “one line of code” demo

Ng shows that the ICA update fits on a single line, to make the point that the hard part is the mathematics rather than the implementation. The line is unreadable unless you have derived it, and deriving it needs maximum likelihood plus a change-of-variables Jacobian — the content of Lecture 16. Take the demo as a promise, not as something you should be able to reproduce this week.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 3 · there is no right answer, so how is anything evaluated?

Supervised learning has held-out error. Unsupervised learning has nothing so clean, and Lecture 1 does not say what replaces it. Three honest options, in increasing order of usefulness: (a) the internal objective itself (distortion for kkk-means) — but it always improves with larger kkk, so it cannot choose kkk; (b) stability — re-run on resampled data and check the groups survive; (c) an extrinsic task — feed the clusters into something you can score. Option (c) is what practitioners actually do.

Gap 4 · choosing kkk

Distortion falls monotonically as kkk grows, reaching zero at k=mk=mk=m. So the plot of distortion against kkk is read not for its minimum but for its elbow, the point after which extra clusters stop buying much. This is a genuinely heuristic step; treat any claim of “the optimal number of clusters” with suspicion unless the model is probabilistic, in which case a likelihood-based criterion can be used instead.

Gap 5 · clustering is not the whole paradigm

Lecture 1 shows clustering and ICA, which makes unsupervised learning look like a bag of tricks. It has three recognisable jobs: grouping (clustering), compression — find a low-dimensional representation that keeps the variance (factor analysis and PCA, Lectures 15–16) — and density estimation, learning p(x)p(x)p(x) itself, which underwrites anomaly detection and every generative model. All three are “find structure”; they differ in what structure means.

03 · Paradigm three

Reinforcement learning

No correct action is ever revealed. Instead you act, the world responds, and occasionally a number arrives telling you how well things are going.

Ng’s framing is the training of a dog. You cannot demonstrate the correct muscle activations; you can only say good dog or bad dog after the fact, and let the animal work out which of its recent choices earned the verdict. Formally the learner interacts with an environment over discrete time: it observes a state sts_{t}st​, chooses an action ata_{t}at​, receives a reward R(st,at)R(s_{t},a_{t})R(st​,at​) and moves to a new state st+1s_{t+1}st+1​. Its goal is to choose actions maximising the expected discounted sum of rewards

E[R(s0,a0)+γR(s1,a1)+γ2R(s2,a2)+⋯],0≤γ<1,\mathbb{E}\Big[R(s_{0},a_{0}) + \gamma R(s_{1},a_{1}) + \gamma^{2}R(s_{2},a_{2}) + \cdots\Big], \qquad 0\le\gamma<1,E[R(s0​,a0​)+γR(s1​,a1​)+γ2R(s2​,a2​)+⋯],0≤γ<1,

and what it outputs is not a prediction but a policy π:S→A\pi:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}π:S→A, a rule saying what to do in every state. The discount factor γ\gammaγ makes the infinite sum finite and encodes impatience: rewards later are worth less than rewards now.

The applications Ng lists — autonomous helicopter aerobatics, quadruped locomotion over rough terrain, game playing — share the property that a human cannot easily demonstrate the right answer but can easily score an attempt. That is precisely the condition under which reinforcement learning is the right tool.

Try it · the reward function is the specification

A robot on a grid. The green square pays +1+1+1, the red square pays −1-1−1, and every ordinary step costs you the step reward below. Slide it and watch the arrows — the optimal policy, recomputed by value iteration each time you move a slider. At a step cost near zero the robot dawdles and takes the safe long way round; make steps expensive and it starts gambling past the pit; make them very expensive and it prefers to end the episode in the pit rather than keep walking. You never told it any of that. You only chose two numbers.

-0.04
0.999

Value iteration converged.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 6 · the credit assignment problem, named

“Good dog” arrives after a hundred muscle movements. Which of them deserved the praise? This is the temporal credit assignment problem, and it is the reason reinforcement learning needs machinery that supervised learning does not — value functions, which propagate a delayed reward backwards through the states that led to it. The demo above shows the propagation directly: switch to Values and watch the +1+1+1 bleed outwards across the grid.

Gap 7 · why this is not just supervised learning with a different loss

Two structural differences. The data depends on the policy: a supervised learner receives a fixed dataset, whereas an agent that never drives left never learns what is on the left. That forces an exploration strategy, with no analogue in Lectures 2–8. Actions have consequences: a supervised prediction changes nothing about the next input, while an action changes the state, so mistakes compound instead of averaging out.

Trap · reward is not the same as the goal

The reward function is a proxy you write down, and the agent will optimise the proxy rather than your intention — exactly what the negative step-reward regime in the demo shows. Anything you forgot to price into RRR is free as far as the agent is concerned. Designing RRR is a modelling problem of the same difficulty as designing features, and gets far less attention.

04 · Cross-cutting

Learning theory and machine-learning strategy

Two questions that apply to every algorithm in the course. Why should fitting the training data help on data you have not seen? And when it does not work, what should you change?

Ng makes an argument here that is easy to miss because it sounds like career advice. It is not: it is the claim that choosing what to do next in a machine-learning project is a technical skill with a theoretical basis, not a matter of taste. A team that trains for six months on more data when the model was underfitting all along has made an error as real as a sign error in a derivative.

The central tension: bias and variance

Suppose your model is doing badly. There are exactly two ways a hypothesis class can be at fault, and they call for opposite remedies.

High bias (underfitting)High variance (overfitting)
Training errorhighlow
Held-out errorhigh, and close to training errormuch higher than training error
Causehypothesis class too smallhypothesis class too large for mmm
More data helps?noyes
Remediesricher features, bigger model, weaker regularisationmore data, fewer features, stronger regularisation

The diagnostic that separates the two cases is the learning curve: plot training error and held-out error against the number of training examples used. The gap between the curves measures variance; the level the training curve settles at measures bias.

What the lecture leaves out

Gap 8 · you need three splits, not two

Lecture 1 speaks loosely of “how well it does on new data”. The discipline that makes that measurable: split your data into a training set (fit θ\thetaθ), a validation or dev set (choose between models, tune hyperparameters), and a test set (report the final number, touched once). The moment you use the test set to make a choice, it becomes a dev set and its estimate becomes optimistic. Everything reported in a paper or a project report should come from a set that influenced no decision.

Gap 9 · what learning theory will actually prove

The lecture asserts that theory tells you “how much data you need”. The shape of the result, which you meet in Lecture 9, is a bound of the form εtest  ≤  εtrain+O ⁣(dm)⏟complexity penalty\varepsilon_{\text{test}} \;\le\; \varepsilon_{\text{train}} + \underbrace{O\!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{d}{m}}\right)}_{\text{complexity penalty}}εtest​≤εtrain​+complexity penaltyO(md​​)​​ holding with high probability, where ddd measures the size of the hypothesis class (its VC dimension) and mmm is the sample size. Read it as a formal statement of Fig. 10: error on unseen data is training error plus a penalty that grows with model richness and shrinks with data. Bias–variance is that inequality in words.

Trap · “my training accuracy is 100 %”

Not evidence of anything. A model with enough parameters can memorise arbitrary labels, and Fig. 9’s right-hand panel has zero training error. The only number that carries information about the future is error on data the fitting procedure never saw.

05 · Cross-cutting

Deep learning, and where it sits

The block students most often mis-file. It belongs on the dashed strip in Fig. 1, not in the row of paradigms above it.

A neural network is a hypothesis class: a parameterised family of functions hθh_{\theta}hθ​ built by composing simple affine maps with elementwise non-linearities. That is all. It slots into the same pipeline as any other class, and it can be trained under any of the three paradigms — supervised (image classification), unsupervised (autoencoders), or reinforcement (policy networks).

Its distinguishing property is that it learns the representation as well as the fit. In Fig. 5 a human chose to add “age” as a second feature; a deep network is a hypothesis class rich enough to construct comparable features for itself from raw input, which is why it dominates domains — images, audio, text — where hand-engineering features is hopeless.

Gap 10 · why the course does linear models first

The order is not historical politeness. Linear regression is the setting in which the cost function is convex, the optimum has a closed form, the probabilistic story is exact, and gradient descent can be understood completely. Every one of those properties is lost in a deep network, so the concepts — hypothesis, cost, gradient, likelihood, regularisation, bias–variance — are best learned where they can be seen clearly. Lectures 11–12 then re-use all of them with the guarantees removed.

08 · Practice

Problems, with full solutions

Work each one on paper before opening it. Problems 5–7 are the ones that actually test whether the taxonomy is understood rather than memorised.

P1Classify each setting as supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement — and if supervised, as regression or classification.

(a) Predicting tomorrow’s electricity demand from the last five years of hourly readings. (b) Given 10 000 unlabelled news articles, grouping them by story. (c) Learning to land a rocket booster in simulation, scored on fuel used and landing accuracy. (d) Deciding whether a credit-card transaction is fraudulent, given a history of transactions labelled by investigators. (e) Given only the transaction history with no labels, flagging unusual transactions.

Solution. (a) Supervised, regression — demand is a real number, and past readings supply their own labels. (b) Unsupervised — clustering. (c) Reinforcement — a scalar score arrives after a sequence of your own control decisions, and no correct thrust profile is ever revealed. (d) Supervised, classification — Y={fraud,legitimate}\mathcal{Y}=\{\text{fraud},\text{legitimate}\}Y={fraud,legitimate}. (e) Unsupervised — anomaly detection via density estimation: learn p(x)p(x)p(x) and flag low-probability points. Note that (d) and (e) are the same task in the same domain, and the paradigm changed only because the labels disappeared. That is the definition doing its work.

P2Write down TTT, EEE and PPP in Mitchell’s sense for a spam filter, then give one bad choice of PPP and say why it is bad.

Solution. TTT: label an incoming email spam or not spam. EEE: a corpus of emails already marked by users. PPP: for instance the misclassification rate on held-out mail.

A bad choice: raw accuracy, when 98 % of mail is legitimate. “Never flag anything” scores 98 % and is worthless. A second, subtler problem is that accuracy weights the two error types equally, while for a user a legitimate mail sent to the spam folder is far more costly than a spam mail left in the inbox. A defensible PPP prices the two mistakes differently — for example, recall on spam subject to a false-positive rate below 0.1%0.1\%0.1%.

P3Fig. 4 shows one feature failing and Fig. 5 shows two features succeeding on the same patients. Does adding a feature ever make a linearly separable dataset non-separable?

Solution. No. If a separating hyperplane w⊤x+b=0w^{\top}x+b=0w⊤x+b=0 exists in Rn\mathbb{R}^{n}Rn, then in Rn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}Rn+1 the hyperplane with weight vector (w,0)(w,0)(w,0) — the old weights plus a zero coefficient on the new feature — separates the same points, because the extra coordinate contributes nothing to the score. So separability can only be preserved or gained, never lost, by adding features.

This is exactly why the SVM story in Lecture 7 is plausible: map into a very high-dimensional space and separability becomes easy. It is also why it is dangerous. Separability in a huge space is cheap, and a model that separates any labelling of the training data has told you nothing about new data — the high-variance panel of Fig. 9 in disguise.

P4Run kkk-means by hand. Points 1,2,3,10,11,121,2,3,10,11,121,2,3,10,11,12 on the line, k=2k=2k=2, initial centroids μ1=2\mu_{1}=2μ1​=2, μ2=3\mu_{2}=3μ2​=3. Give the assignments and centroids at every step until convergence, and the final distortion.

Solution.

Iteration 1, assign. Distances to μ1=2\mu_{1}=2μ1​=2 and μ2=3\mu_{2}=3μ2​=3: point 1 → cluster 1; point 2 → cluster 1; point 3 → cluster 2; points 10, 11, 12 → cluster 2 (all nearer to 3 than to 2). So C1={1,2}C_{1}=\{1,2\}C1​={1,2}, C2={3,10,11,12}C_{2}=\{3,10,11,12\}C2​={3,10,11,12}.

Iteration 1, update. μ1=1+22=1.5\mu_{1}=\tfrac{1+2}{2}=1.5μ1​=21+2​=1.5, μ2=3+10+11+124=9\mu_{2}=\tfrac{3+10+11+12}{4}=9μ2​=43+10+11+12​=9.

Iteration 2, assign. Point 3 is at distance 1.51.51.5 from μ1\mu_1μ1​ and 666 from μ2\mu_2μ2​, so it moves: C1={1,2,3}C_{1}=\{1,2,3\}C1​={1,2,3}, C2={10,11,12}C_{2}=\{10,11,12\}C2​={10,11,12}.

Iteration 2, update. μ1=2\mu_{1}=2μ1​=2, μ2=11\mu_{2}=11μ2​=11.

Iteration 3, assign. No assignment changes — converged.

Distortion =∑i∥x(i)−μc(i)∥2=(1+0+1)+(1+0+1)=4=\sum_{i}\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{c^{(i)}}\rVert^{2}=(1{+}0{+}1)+(1{+}0{+}1)=4=∑i​∥x(i)−μc(i)​∥2=(1+0+1)+(1+0+1)=4.

Worth noticing: the initialisation put both centroids inside the left-hand blob, and the algorithm still recovered. With μ1=1,μ2=2\mu_{1}=1,\mu_{2}=2μ1​=1,μ2​=2 it also recovers; with three tightly grouped blobs and k=3k=3k=3 it often does not, which is the point of the Re-seed button in the demo.

P5In the gridworld demo, why does a large negative step reward make the agent walk deliberately into the −1-1−1 pit? Answer with the discounted return, not with intuition.

Solution. Reaching either terminal square ends the episode, so the agent’s choice is between two total returns. Let rrr be the step reward, γ\gammaγ the discount, and suppose the pit is dpd_{p}dp​ steps away and the goal dgd_{g}dg​ steps away, with dp<dgd_{p}<d_{g}dp​<dg​. Ending in the pit is worth roughly r1−γdp1−γ+γdp(−1),r\frac{1-\gamma^{d_{p}}}{1-\gamma}+\gamma^{d_{p}}(-1),r1−γ1−γdp​​+γdp​(−1), and reaching the goal roughly r1−γdg1−γ+γdg(+1).r\frac{1-\gamma^{d_{g}}}{1-\gamma}+\gamma^{d_{g}}(+1).r1−γ1−γdg​​+γdg​(+1). With γ\gammaγ close to 1 the accumulated step cost is about r dr\,drd, so the comparison is r dp−1r\,d_{p}-1rdp​−1 against r dg+1r\,d_{g}+1rdg​+1. Since r<0r<0r<0, the first is larger whenever ∣r∣(dg−dp)>2|r|(d_{g}-d_{p})>2∣r∣(dg​−dp​)>2: once each step hurts more than the 222-point swing between pit and goal, the fastest exit wins, and the fastest exit is the pit.

The lesson is the one in Gap 7’s trap: the agent optimised exactly what you wrote down. You wrote down that living is expensive.

P6A classmate reports 99.2 % training accuracy and 71 % held-out accuracy on the tumour data, using 400 features and 300 examples. Diagnose, and rank three interventions.

Solution. A 28-point gap between training and held-out accuracy with n>mn>mn>m is the signature of high variance: the hypothesis class is large enough to fit the training set almost exactly, including its noise. Bias is evidently not the problem — training error is near zero.

Ranked by expected return per unit of effort: (1) regularise, or cut the feature set — cheap, immediate, and directly attacks the diagnosed cause; (2) collect more labelled examples — effective for variance (left panel of Fig. 10) but slow and expensive; (3) switch to a more expressive model — the wrong move, since it increases variance further. The one thing to do first, before any of them, is plot the learning curve: if the gap is still closing steeply at m=300m=300m=300, option (2) is worth more than it looks.

P7You have 10 000 labelled images and want to report a single accuracy figure in your project write-up. Describe the protocol, and name the failure that a train/test split alone does not prevent.

Solution. Split three ways — say 60 % train, 20 % dev, 20 % test, drawn at random so all three follow the same distribution. Fit parameters on train. Choose every hyperparameter (model family, regularisation strength, feature set, stopping point) by dev-set error. Evaluate on test exactly once, at the end, and report that number.

The failure a two-way split does not prevent is selection bias from repeated evaluation. If you tune against the test set, then after twenty tries you have chosen the model that best fits that particular sample’s noise, and your reported figure is optimistic by an amount that grows with the number of comparisons. The test set is a measuring instrument, and reading it changes it.

09 · Prep

Exam and interview questions

Short-answer form. Say the answer aloud before reading it.

Conceptual

What single property of the data determines whether a problem is supervised or unsupervised?

The presence of targets y(i)y^{(i)}y(i) in the training set. Not the algorithm, not the model, not the domain.

Is logistic regression a regression algorithm?

No — it is a classification algorithm. It is named for the regression it performs on the log-odds, which is a statement about its internals, not about its output space.

Give a problem that is regression under one performance measure and classification under another.

Predicting a patient’s tumour size in centimetres is regression; predicting whether that size exceeds 3 cm is classification. The underlying quantity is the same; discretising the target changes the paradigm, the loss and the algorithm.

Why can training error not be used to choose kkk in kkk-means?

Distortion decreases monotonically in kkk and hits zero at k=mk=mk=m, so minimising it selects one cluster per point. Use an elbow, a stability criterion, or a downstream task.

Is deep learning a fourth learning paradigm?

No. It is a family of hypothesis classes, usable within supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning.

State the i.i.d. assumption and name one deployment scenario that violates it.

Training and test examples are drawn independently from a single fixed distribution D\mathcal{D}D. Violated by any distribution shift: a spam filter trained on last year’s mail, a vision system trained in daylight and deployed at night, or any setting where the model’s own predictions change the data it later receives.

Your training and dev errors are both 26 % and you need 5 %. Should you collect more data?

No. Equal, high errors are a bias signature; the right-hand panel of Fig. 10. More data will not move a curve that has already flattened. Enrich the model or the features.

Applied

You are asked to build a system that recommends a treatment plan; you have historical records of what doctors prescribed and how patients fared. How would you pose this?

Both framings are defensible and the choice matters. As supervised learning: predict the doctor’s prescription from the patient record — easy to train, but it can at best imitate current practice, including its mistakes. As reinforcement learning: treat outcome as reward and the treatment sequence as actions — it can in principle exceed current practice, but the data was collected under the doctors’ policy, not the learner’s, which is the off-policy problem. Naming that tension is the answer the question is looking for.

A product manager asks for “an AI that finds interesting patterns in our logs”. What do you ask back?

What decision will the output change? Unsupervised learning has no intrinsic notion of interesting, so the objective has to be imported from the use case: grouping (segments to target), compression (a representation to feed downstream), or density estimation (anomalies to alert on). Without that, no criterion exists by which the result could be judged correct.

Why do practitioners keep using linear models when deep networks exist?

Sample efficiency, interpretability and diagnosability. With small mmm a linear model is on the good side of the bias–variance trade; its coefficients are inspectable, which matters where a decision must be justified; and it trains fast enough to iterate on the data, which is usually where the real gains are.

10 · Corrections

Eight things students get wrong

Collected from the way this material is usually mis-remembered.

  1. “Regression means fitting a line.” Regression means the target is continuous. A regression model can be a deep network; a classifier can be a straight line.
  2. “Logistic regression is regression.” It is classification. The name describes the linear model sitting on the log-odds inside it.
  3. “Deep learning is a fourth paradigm.” It is a hypothesis class. See Fig. 1.
  4. “Unsupervised learning means clustering.” Clustering is one of three jobs, alongside dimensionality reduction and density estimation.
  5. “More features can only help.” They can only help the training error. Held-out error has a minimum in the middle.
  6. “x(i)x^{(i)}x(i) is xxx to the power iii.” Parenthesised superscripts index examples; subscripts index features.
  7. “The algorithm learns the model.” You choose the hypothesis class; the algorithm chooses the parameters inside it. Fig. 3 is one dataset with two different models and no way for the data to decide between them.
  8. “Reinforcement learning is supervised learning with a delayed label.” Two extra difficulties have no supervised counterpart: the agent's own actions determine what data it ever sees, and credit for a reward must be assigned back across time.
